title: the scope of the answer in the interface and in ACP
intent: The wave is the third of the track C of the catch-up plan (the areas of the approval): the core (C1) named the scope of an answer, C2 gave every scope exactly one carrier, and this wave gives the surfaces that scope.  The dictionary of the answers was `(:once :always :reject)' -- two names that remembered and one that did not -- and the word `always' meant three different things: the file of the user in the plain path, the memory of the run in the attached path and the memory of the session in the ACP path.  The dictionary of the answers is now the dictionary of the scopes: `(:once :session :project :global :reject)'.  The answer `once' is this call and is forgotten, the answer `session' is the carrier of the path that asks, the answer `project' is the file of the project and the answer `global' is the file of the user; the scope `run' is not an answer, because a person is never asked to make a rule that dies with the run.  The legacy name `always' is an alias of the answer `session' and is written in one place next to the dictionary (`yeah-approval--legacy-replies' in `lib/yeah-approval.el'); it is NOT an alias of the answer `global', because reading it as `global' would move the rule of the attached path out of the memory of the run and into the file of the user -- a change of behaviour that no document asks for, and one that contradicts the claims `an-answer-carries-a-scope' and `a-scope-decides-where-the-rule-lives' and the record of the wave C1.  The shared approval view now offers the four scopes and the refusal and names what every answer allows; the wire of ACP carries the same five answers as the options of `session/request_permission' (`allow-once', `allow-session', `allow-project', `allow-global', `reject-once'; the kinds stay the kinds of ACP -- `allow_once', `allow_always', `reject_once'), and the schema of the wire declares the method of the question with the params the kernel sends and the result it reads.  The scope of an answer reaches the rule the answer writes: the rule of the answer `session' lives in the carrier of the path that asks, the rule of the answer `project' lives in the file of the project and in no other carrier, and the rule of the answer `global' lives in the file of the user.  A decision that names a scope its answer does not name comes back as a refusal that names the scope and the carrier.  The claim of the wave is new (`the-question-offers-the-scope').
objection: What the wave does not prove, and its price is named.  (a) **The plain path has no session of its own**: the carrier of the plain path is `global' (the file of the user), so the answer `session' and the answer `global' coincide there -- both write the file of the user, and the scope of the answer `session' in that path is the scope of that carrier.  The wave says so in the docstrings and invents no second meaning of the plain path; a reader of the view sees the two answers and must know that they land in one place there.  (b) **Two names that are close and are not the same**: the command `yeah-approval-allow-always' (the key `a') is the answer `global' -- the explicit forever of the person -- while the legacy REPLY `always' (the Elisp spelling and the wire name `allow-always') is the answer `session'.  The decision of the view carries the reply as it was given, so the legacy spelling still reaches the kernel unchanged; a reader of the code can meet both names in one file and must read the docstrings to tell them apart.  (c) **The method of the question sits in the table of the methods**: `session/request_permission' is a request of the agent to the client, and the dispatcher of the agent now knows it and refuses it by name with `-32602'.  The alternative -- a separate table of the requests from the agent to the client -- contradicts the decision D6 of the brief and was not taken.  (d) **The tension between C1 and the reach of the file of the project**: C1 demanded that a decision which names `:scope :project' in the run path is refused, and the file of the project is reachable from every path.  The resolution is that the REPLY decides the scope and a decision that names a scope its answer does not name is refused -- but a reader of the two records must read both to see that the refusal and the reach do not contradict each other.  (e) **The file of the project is written without asking**: the answer `project' creates `.yeah/rules.json' of the project, and the wave does not ask the person whether the project may hold such a file.  (f) **The API `yeah-perm-record-decision' (`save: 'always') has no callers and was left as it is**: it is the old way of remembering an answer and `lib/yeah-perm.el' is not a file of this wave.  (g) **The wave did not fix the texts outside its files**: the parent fixed three stale texts afterwards (`lib/yeah-turn.el', `lib/yeah-product.el' and the header of the check of C1), and the picture of the approval view changes as well -- the render of the interface names the offers now, and the pixel check needs a screen and is not in the list of the checks of the wave.
refuted_by: The question offers no scope, or a scope that is not one of the four; the wire carries a name that names no scope; the legacy name `always' is not read as an answer; the scope of the answer does not reach the rule the answer writes; or the schema of the wire does not declare the method of the question.
note: The wave is the third of the track C (the areas of the approval): the core (C1), the carriers (C2) and the surfaces (C3).  (1) **The decisions of the parent are named and dated** (2026-11-22): the dictionary of the answers is the dictionary of the scopes, `(:once :session :project :global :reject)'; the scope `run' is not an answer; the legacy name `always' is an alias of the answer `session' and not of the answer `global', and the reason is the scope: reading `always' as `global' would move the rule of the attached path out of the memory of the run and into the file of the user; the alias is written in one place next to the dictionary and nowhere else; the interface offers four answers and the refusal; the wire carries the same areas in the identifiers of the options (`allow-once', `allow-session', `allow-project', `allow-global', `reject-once') and the kinds of ACP stay as they are (`allow_once', `allow_always', `reject_once'); the scope of an answer reaches the rule the answer writes, and a decision that names a scope its answer does not name is refused by name.  (2) **The measurement is a real move**: the check of the wave (524 lines) opens the view and answers it through the command of the view, runs a run with a fake transport (a fake model, not a mock of the kernel), and travels the question and the answer over the wire as the text of the protocol; it works in three temporary directories (the project, the configuration of the user and the data home) and binds the carrier of the configuration and the root of the project to them, so it writes nothing into the machine of the person.  (3) **The controls bite, measured on the merged tree by the parent** (2026-11-22) and taken from `spec.json' as the rule of the method demands (§16.101): the control of the new claim `sed -i 's/(:project :project)/(:project :global)/' lib/yeah-approval.el' makes the check of the wave fail with its own refusals (`the rule of the project landed in the file of the user', `the answer that came back over the wire carries the scope :global, not :project') -- exit 1; the honest tree -- exit 0.  (4) **The control of the amended claim `approvals-have-reply-kinds' was dead and was replaced**: the registered control `sed -i 's|(when (eq kind :always)|(when (eq kind :never)|' lib/yeah-approval.el' looked for a literal that the rewrite of the wave removed -- the alias of the legacy name is written in one place next to the dictionary, so there is no second `when' that mentions `:always'.  The replacement `sed -i 's/(("always" . "session"))/(("always" . "global"))/' lib/yeah-approval.el' was measured on the merged tree: it breaks the second half of the amended claim in three checks (the legacy answer is not the answer `session') -- exit 1 each, and the honest tree -- exit 0.  Only the `control' changed; the text, the falsifier, the id, the requirements, the owner, the phase, the register and the waiver are the former ones, and the scope grew because the subject of the claim grew (§16.101).  (5) **Two claims were amended**: `one-approval-surface' (the view now names what it offers, and the scopes it offers are named in the text and in the falsifier) and `approvals-have-reply-kinds' (the answers are the scopes, and the rule of an answer lives in the carrier of that scope).  Both keep their ids, their requirements, their owners and their controls, and both grew in scope, because the wave touched the files they speak of.  (6) **The wave moved nine references of the picture of the layers**: the picture named the lines of the code that the waves B2, B3, C2 and C3 moved (`lib/yeah-scheduler.el', `lib/yeah-approval.el', `lib/yeah-perm.el', `lib/yeah-process.el', `lib/yeah-files.el', `lib/yeah-delegate.el', `lib/yeah-service-ui.el', `lib/yeah-acp.el', `lib/yeah-approval-ui.el'); the parent traced every one of them to the definition it named and re-bound the nine anchors (the precedent of the commit `da8f6ea`), and the check of the picture is green.  (7) **Two stale texts were found by the wave and fixed by the parent**: `lib/yeah-turn.el' said that the reply of the person is `:once' or `:always'', and the check of C1 said that a scope without a carrier is refused by name -- after the wave the scope `project' HAS a carrier, and the check measures something else: a decision that names a scope its answer does not name.  The check was still green; only the text was wrong, and the text is what a reader trusts.
